Privacy Policy

1. Controller

The controller within the meaning of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is:

Crodox Software GmbH
An der Mauer 4
73479 Ellwangen/Jagst
Germany
info@crodox.com

If you have any questions about data protection or wish to exercise your rights, you can contact us at any time using the email address stated above.

2. General Information on Data Processing

We process personal data only to the extent necessary to provide our website and services, process inquiries, manage user accounts where applicable, send our newsletter, analyze website usage, or comply with legal obligations.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.

Processing is carried out in particular on the basis of:

- Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR where you have given your consent;
- Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR where processing is necessary for the performance of a contract or for taking pre-contractual measures;
- Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR where we are legally obliged to process data; and
- Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR where we have a legitimate interest in the processing and your interests or fundamental rights do not override that interest.

Where we use cookies or comparable technologies, we also comply with the requirements of the German Telecommunications Digital Services Data Protection Act (TDDDG). Technically necessary storage or access is based on Section 25(2) TDDDG. Non-essential storage or access, in particular for analytics or marketing purposes, is based on your consent pursuant to Section 25(1) TDDDG.

3. What Personal Data We Collect

Depending on how you use our website and services, we may process the following categories of personal data:

- Contact details, such as your name and email address;
- Account data, where user accounts are offered, such as email address, login credentials, username, account settings, and voluntary profile information;
- Communication data, such as the content of messages you send to us via contact forms or email;
- Newsletter data, such as email address, name where provided, registration time, IP address at registration, confirmation status, and newsletter interaction data where consent has been given;
- Technical data, such as IP address, date and time of access, pages accessed, referrer URL, browser type, operating system, device information, and log file data;
- Usage and analytics data, where you have given your consent, such as pages visited, duration of visit, click behavior, approximate location data, device and browser information, and interactions with our website;
- Consent data, such as your consent choices, time of consent, consent status, and withdrawal of consent;
- Billing or contract-related data, if paid services are offered in the future, such as billing address, payment status, and contractual information.

We do not intentionally collect special categories of personal data within the meaning of Art. 9 GDPR unless this is expressly required in an individual case and a valid legal basis exists.

4. Provision of the Website and Server Log Files

When you access our website, technically necessary data is processed in order to display the website and ensure its stability and security. This may include, in particular, your IP address, date and time of access, pages accessed, referrer URL, browser type, operating system, and amount of data transferred.

The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR. Our legitimate interest lies in the secure, stable, and error-free provision of our website. Where technically necessary cookies or comparable technologies are used for this purpose, this is done on the basis of Section 25(2) TDDDG.

We use Vercel Inc. as our hosting provider. Vercel hosts and delivers our website, including frontend content, static assets, and technical infrastructure components required for the operation of the website. In this context, Vercel may process technical data, server log files, IP addresses, and request metadata.

Where Vercel processes personal data on our behalf, such processing is carried out on the basis of the applicable data protection terms provided by Vercel. We will conclude a data processing agreement or Data Processing Addendum with Vercel where this is required under Art. 28 GDPR.

Server log files are generally stored only for as long as necessary to ensure the security, stability, and proper functioning of the website. A longer storage period may apply if this is necessary to investigate security incidents, prevent abuse, comply with legal obligations, or establish, exercise, or defend legal claims.

5. Contact Form

If you contact us via the contact form, we process the data you enter, in particular your name, email address, and message content, in order to process and respond to your inquiry.

The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR if your inquiry is related to a contract or pre-contractual measures. In all other cases, processing is carried out on the basis of Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR. Our legitimate interest lies in efficiently processing inquiries and communicating with users of our website.

For the technical processing and sending of messages from the contact form, we use Resend, a service provided by Plus Five Five, Inc., USA. The data entered in the contact form and technical email metadata may be transmitted to and processed by Resend.

Where Resend processes personal data on our behalf, such processing is carried out on the basis of the applicable data protection terms provided by Resend. We will conclude a data processing agreement or Data Processing Addendum with Resend where this is required under Art. 28 GDPR.

Processing of personal data in the USA cannot be excluded. Where personal data is transferred to the USA or other third countries, we rely on appropriate safeguards such as an adequacy decision, certification under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, Standard Contractual Clauses of the European Commission, or another valid transfer mechanism under Art. 44 et seq. GDPR.

We store contact inquiries only for as long as necessary to process your inquiry. In general, contact inquiries are deleted after final completion of the inquiry, unless statutory retention obligations apply or longer storage is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims.

6. Newsletter

You can subscribe to our newsletter on our website. For registration, we process in particular your email address. Depending on the form, your name, the time of registration, your IP address, and information relating to the confirmation of your registration may also be processed.

The newsletter is used to send you information, updates, and news about Crodox, our products, development tools, and related topics.

Subscription to the newsletter is based on your consent pursuant to Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR. Where technically necessary information is stored or accessed in connection with registration or sending, this is additionally based on Section 25(2) TDDDG.

Where analytics or tracking technologies are used in the newsletter, for example to measure open or click rates, this is done only on the basis of your consent pursuant to Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR and, where required, Section 25(1) TDDDG.

For sending and managing our newsletter, we use Mailchimp, a service provided by The Rocket Science Group LLC d/b/a Mailchimp, USA. If you subscribe to the newsletter, your data will be transmitted to and processed by Mailchimp. Mailchimp may process, in particular, your email address, registration data, technical information, and interactions with the newsletter.

Where Mailchimp processes personal data on our behalf, such processing is carried out on the basis of the applicable data protection terms provided by Mailchimp. We will conclude a data processing agreement or Data Processing Addendum with Mailchimp where this is required under Art. 28 GDPR.

Mailchimp may also process personal data in the USA. Mailchimp states that it uses, among other mechanisms, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and Standard Contractual Clauses within the framework of its data protection terms for data transfers.

You may withdraw your consent to receive the newsletter at any time with effect for the future by using the unsubscribe link in each newsletter email or by contacting us directly.

After you unsubscribe, your email address will generally be deleted from the active newsletter mailing list. We may store proof of registration, including consent status, registration time, confirmation time, and IP address, where this is necessary to document a previously given consent or to defend against legal claims.

7. User Account and Registration

If you create a user account for our services, we process the data required to create, manage, secure, and provide the account. This may include, in particular, your email address, login credentials, username, technical protocol data, account settings, and any additional voluntary information you provide.

The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR where processing is necessary for the creation, administration, and use of the user account and the related services. Where processing is based on your consent, the legal basis is Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR. Where processing is necessary for security, fraud prevention, or service improvement, the legal basis may be Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR.

Our service is not specifically directed at children under the age of 16. Minors may create and use an account only if they are legally permitted to do so or if their legal representatives have consented to such use.

Account data is stored for as long as the user account exists. After deletion of the account, the data will generally be deleted unless statutory retention obligations apply or longer storage is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims.

8. Google Analytics

We use Google Analytics, a web analytics service provided by Google Ireland Limited, Gordon House, Barrow Street, Dublin 4, Ireland. Google Analytics helps us understand how visitors use our website so that we can improve content, functionality, and user experience.

Google Analytics may use cookies and comparable technologies and process information about the use of our website. This may include, in particular, pages visited, duration of visit, click behavior, referrer URL, device and browser information, approximate location data, and IP address. Processing may also be carried out by Google companies outside the European Union or the European Economic Area, in particular in the USA.

Google Analytics is used only if you have previously given your consent via our consent banner. The legal basis for accessing information on your device or storing information on your device is Section 25(1) TDDDG. The legal basis for the subsequent processing of personal data is Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR.

You can withdraw your consent at any time with effect for the future via the cookie or consent settings on our website. As long as no consent has been given, Google Analytics will not be loaded for analytics purposes.

Google requires certain information and consents for users in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland when Google products are used. Where required, we transmit your consent decision to Google, in particular within the framework of Google Consent Mode. This may include information about whether consent has been granted or denied for analytics storage, ad storage, ad user data, and ad personalization, depending on the configuration used.

In this context, Google may process consent information and related technical information as an independent controller. Further information on Google's processing activities can be found in Google's privacy information and the terms applicable to Google Analytics.

Analytics data is retained in accordance with the retention settings configured in Google Analytics. We configure retention periods in a privacy-friendly manner and retain analytics data only for as long as necessary for analysis and website improvement, unless you withdraw your consent earlier or a shorter period is technically applied.

9. Cookies and Comparable Technologies

Our website may use cookies and comparable technologies. Cookies are small pieces of information stored on your device. Comparable technologies may store or access information on your device.

Technically necessary cookies and technologies are used to provide the website, enable security functions, remember privacy settings, or perform functions requested by you. The legal basis is Section 25(2) TDDDG and, where personal data is processed, Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR.

Non-essential cookies and technologies, in particular for analytics or marketing purposes, are used only after your prior consent. The legal basis is Section 25(1) TDDDG and Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR.

You can withdraw your consent at any time with effect for the future via our cookie or consent settings.

Consent records may be stored for the duration necessary to document your consent choices and to comply with legal accountability obligations. Where consent is withdrawn, the withdrawal is recorded to ensure that your choice is respected.

10. Minors

Our website and services are not directed at children under the age of 16. We do not knowingly ask children under the age of 16 to provide us with personal data.

Where we process personal data on the basis of consent, in particular for newsletter subscriptions, analytics or marketing cookies, or comparable voluntary functions, valid consent can generally only be given by users who are at least 16 years old. Users under the age of 16 may only provide such consent if consent is given or authorized by their legal representatives.

Depending on how a minor uses our website or services, the personal data processed may include contact details, email address, newsletter registration data, account data, technical data, communication data, and consent data. We process such data only where a valid legal basis exists, such as verifiable parental consent, performance of a contract where legally permissible, compliance with legal obligations, or legitimate interests that do not override the rights and interests of the minor.

If we become aware that personal data of a child under the age of 16 has been provided to us without the required consent of the legal representatives and no other legal basis applies, we will delete the relevant data.

Personal data of minors is retained only for as long as necessary for the respective purpose. Newsletter data is retained only for as long as the subscription exists, unless proof of consent must be retained. Account data is retained only for as long as the account exists, unless statutory retention obligations or legal claims require longer storage. Contact inquiries are retained only for as long as necessary to process the inquiry and for appropriate documentation.

Parents or legal guardians may contact us at any time at info@crodox.com if they believe that their child has provided us with personal data without their consent. They may request information about the data processed and, where legally applicable, request correction, deletion, restriction of processing, or object to processing.

11. External Links

Our website may contain links to external websites. When you click on an external link, you leave our website. The respective providers are solely responsible for the processing of personal data on the linked websites. Please refer to their respective privacy policies.

12. Recipients of Personal Data

We disclose personal data only if this is necessary to provide our website and services, if you have given your consent, if there is a legal obligation, or if we have a legitimate interest.

Recipients of personal data may include, in particular:

- hosting and infrastructure providers, including Vercel;
- Resend for the technical processing and sending of contact form messages;
- Mailchimp for newsletter sending and newsletter management;
- Google Analytics or Google Ireland Limited for website analytics after consent;
- cookie or consent management providers, where used;
- technical service providers and processors;
- payment or billing providers, if paid services are offered in the future;
- authorities, courts, tax advisors, auditors, or legal advisors, where legally required or necessary for legal enforcement.

13. Transfers to Third Countries

Some of the service providers we use are based in the USA or may process personal data in the USA or other third countries. A different level of data protection may apply there than in the European Union.

Where personal data is transferred to third countries, this is done only if there is a suitable legal basis, such as an adequacy decision, certification under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, Standard Contractual Clauses of the European Commission, your explicit consent, or another valid transfer mechanism under Art. 44 et seq. GDPR.

14. Storage Period

We store personal data only for as long as necessary for the respective purposes. Thereafter, the data will be deleted unless statutory retention obligations apply or longer storage is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims.

The following retention principles apply:

- Server log files are generally stored only for as long as necessary for security, stability, troubleshooting, and abuse prevention.
- Contact form inquiries are generally stored until the inquiry has been fully processed and for an appropriate documentation period thereafter.
- Newsletter data is stored for as long as you are subscribed to the newsletter.
- After unsubscribing from the newsletter, your email address will generally be removed from the active mailing list. Proof of consent may be retained where necessary to document consent or defend against legal claims.
- Consent records are stored for as long as necessary to demonstrate compliance with legal accountability obligations.
- Account data is stored for as long as the account exists. After account deletion, data is deleted unless statutory retention obligations or legal claims require longer storage.
- Analytics data is processed in accordance with the retention settings configured in Google Analytics and only within the scope of your consent.
- Data required under commercial or tax law may be retained for the statutory retention periods.
- Data relevant to legal claims may be retained for the duration of the applicable limitation periods.

15. Automated Decision-Making and Profiling

We do not carry out automated decision-making or profiling within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR.

16. Your Rights

Subject to the statutory requirements, you have the following rights:

- right of access to the personal data processed by us;
- right to rectification of inaccurate or incomplete data;
- right to erasure of your personal data;
- right to restriction of processing;
- right to data portability;
- right to object to processing based on Art. 6(1)(e) or Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR;
- right to withdraw consent with effect for the future;
- right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority.

If you have given consent, you may withdraw it at any time with effect for the future. The lawfulness of processing carried out before withdrawal remains unaffected.

To exercise your rights, you can contact us at info@crodox.com.

17. Right to Lodge a Complaint with a Supervisory Authority

If you believe that the processing of your personal data violates data protection law, you have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority. In particular, you may contact the supervisory authority responsible for your habitual residence, place of work, or the place of the alleged infringement.

18. Data Security

We take appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data against loss, misuse, unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, and destruction. Our security measures are continuously adapted in line with technological developments.

19. Changes to this Privacy Policy

We may amend this Privacy Policy if legal requirements, technical functions, or our data processing activities change. The current version is available on our website.

posts.title: How Anthropic Accidentally Leaked 500,000 Lines of Code
posts.subtitle: And What It Means for Every Enterprise Using AI
posts.author: Crodox

blocks.alt: The Anthropic Claude Code leak - March 31, 2026
blocks.caption: The Anthropic Claude Code leak - March 31, 2026

blocks.text: On March 31, 2026, Anthropic, one of the world's leading AI safety companies and the creator of Claude, accidentally published a portion of internal code of its flagship product, Claude Code, to a public npm registry. Over 512,000 lines of proprietary TypeScript across nearly 2,000 files were exposed. Within hours, the code was mirrored, dissected, rewritten in Python and Rust, and studied by tens of thousands of developers.
Anthropic called it "a release packaging issue caused by human error, not a security breach." That's technically accurate, it obscures far more significant, strategic, and operational problems.
This wasn't a hack. It was something far more uncomfortable: a process failure hiding in plain sight - the kind that could happen to any enterprise using AI coding tools today.

The culprit was a JavaScript source map file, a debugging artifact that developers use internally, accidentally bundled into a public release of Claude Code version 2.1.88. That file pointed to a zip archive hosted on Anthropic's own cloud storage, containing significant parts of the client-side agent logic behind Claude Code.
What was exposed:

items: Complete orchestration and agent logic - how Claude Code manages long-running tasks
Memory management system and context handling across complex sessions
Feature flags for dozens of unreleased capabilities, fully built but not yet shipped
Internal model codenames (Capybara, Mythos, Fennec) and performance metrics

blocks.text: Security researcher Chaofan Shou spotted it almost immediately and posted about it publicly. The tweet was viewed over 30 million times. By the time Anthropic issued takedowns, the code had already been mirrored into thousands of repositories. The company eventually issued over 8,000 copyright takedown requests, some of which hit legitimate forks by mistake, forcing an embarrassing partial rollback.

"The takedowns didn't contain the leak. They just changed its file extension."
- Jeff Brown, IANS Faculty

To make matters worse, the leak coincided almost exactly with a separate, unrelated supply chain attack on the axios npm package - meaning developers who updated Claude Code during a specific three-hour window may have also inadvertently installed a Remote Access Trojan.

This was not Anthropic's first incident. In February 2025, an early version of Claude Code had leaked in a nearly identical way. And just days before March 31, a confidential draft blog post about an unreleased model had also been exposed. Three significant security lapses in just over a year.
It would be easy to treat this as an Anthropic-specific story - a cautionary tale about one company moving too fast. But that reading is dangerously comfortable.
The real lesson is universal. It cuts to the heart of what happens when AI tools are given broad, ungoverned access to your codebase.

blocks.alt: The structural problems that made this leak possible - and inevitable
blocks.caption: The structural problems that made this leak possible - and inevitable

blocks.text: Claude Code, like all modern AI coding agents, works by taking in large amounts of code context and using it to generate, modify, and deploy changes. The more context it has, the better it performs. But that same breadth of access - which makes the tool powerful - is precisely what makes a packaging mishap this catastrophic.
Now ask yourself: what would the equivalent look like inside your organization?
Your AI coding tools have access to:

items: Your entire codebase, including internal APIs and business logic
Your unreleased product roadmap, embedded in code comments and feature flags
Your performance metrics and internal model benchmarks
Your security architecture and access control logic

blocks.text: All of it is sitting there, accessible, because that's how these tools are designed to work. When the release process fails - as human processes inevitably do - there is nothing to contain the blast radius.

"What leaked matters more than the fact that it leaked. This exposed proprietary techniques that took years and billions of dollars to build."
- Jeff Brown, IANS Faculty

blocks.heading: How Crodox Would Have Prevented This

blocks.text: This is precisely the problem Crodox was built to solve.

blocks.alt: Without Crodox: full exposure. With Crodox: zero exposure
blocks.caption: Without Crodox: full exposure. With Crodox: zero exposure

blocks.text: At the core of the Crodox platform is code isolation per change. Instead of giving AI agents - or any developer, internal or external - access to the full codebase, Crodox automatically extracts only the specific code relevant to a given task, including all its dependencies, across languages.

Applied to the Anthropic scenario: if Claude Code's release pipeline had been running through Crodox, the packaging process would have operated on a scoped, controlled extract of the relevant release files - not the full source tree. The debugging source map would never have been in scope. It wouldn't have been accessible. It couldn't have leaked.
Crodox delivers three core protections:

items: Code Isolation per Change - AI agents and pipelines only see what's relevant to the task at hand
Governed Development Scopes - humans and AI work in controlled environments, never the full codebase
Safe Reintegration - validated changes are automatically merged back, with no manual shortcuts possible

blocks.text: The Anthropic incident happened because someone took a shortcut that bypassed normal release safeguards. Crodox makes those shortcuts structurally impossible - not by adding more rules, but by making the correct path the only available path.

Anthropic is not a careless company. They are, by most accounts, one of the most safety-conscious organisations in the AI industry. And yet they have now leaked parts of their own source code twice, exposed a confidential model roadmap, and accidentally nuked thousands of GitHub repositories, all within a matter of weeks.
If it can happen to them, it can happen to anyone.

The uncomfortable truth is that AI coding tools fundamentally change the risk profile of software development. They're powerful precisely because they operate with broad access and high autonomy. But that power comes with a corresponding responsibility to govern that access carefully.
The AI coding wave is here. The question isn't whether you'll use these tools - you will, or your competitors will. The question is whether you'll build the infrastructure to use them safely.
That infrastructure is what Crodox provides.

posts.title: Reflections from GITEX AI Europe Berlin
posts.subtitle: The Future of AI-Assisted Software Development Is Taking Shape
posts.author: Crodox

blocks.text: Last week, the Crodox team had the opportunity to attend GITEX AI Europe in Berlin, one of Europe's fastest-growing events for artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. It brought together thousands of CTOs, software engineers, founders, enterprise leaders, researchers, and AI practitioners - all focused on one question: How do we turn AI into real business value?

For us, the event was much more than an exhibition. It was an opportunity to validate the challenges we see every day when speaking with engineering organizations and to understand where the industry is heading.
One theme was impossible to miss: organizations are no longer asking whether they should adopt AI - they are asking how to deploy it responsibly and at scale.
Across countless conversations, we heard similar questions:

items: How can AI accelerate software development without sacrificing quality?
How do we maintain security and compliance when AI contributes to production code?
How can engineering teams keep developers in control while benefiting from increasingly capable AI agents?
What does an effective human-in-the-loop workflow actually look like?

blocks.text: These are exactly the problems Crodox was built to solve.

blocks.heading: Strong Resonance for the Crodox Approach

blocks.text: One of the biggest highlights of the event was seeing how strongly the Crodox platform resonated with visitors.

Whether we spoke with startups building AI-first products or large enterprises navigating strict governance requirements, the feedback was remarkably consistent. Organizations want AI to make developers more productive - but they also need transparency, oversight, and confidence before code reaches production.

The concept of enabling developers and AI agents to work efficiently on isolated parts of a codebase while embedding human review and compliance directly into the workflow generated many engaging discussions.

It reinforced our belief that the future isn't about replacing developers with AI. It's about creating workflows where humans and AI collaborate effectively, allowing teams to innovate faster while maintaining the standards required for enterprise software.
As AI capabilities continue to improve, one thing became increasingly clear throughout the event: human review is becoming a competitive advantage rather than a bottleneck.
Organizations are looking for solutions that combine:

items: Faster software delivery
High-quality code generation
Built-in governance and compliance
Transparent review processes
Developer control throughout the development lifecycle

blocks.text: The conversation is shifting away from "Can AI write code?" toward "How do we safely integrate AI into our engineering processes?"
That shift aligns perfectly with Crodox's vision.
We would like to thank everyone who visited our booth, shared their challenges, demonstrated their AI initiatives, and explored how Crodox can support modern software development.
The openness of the discussions, the thoughtful questions, and the willingness to exchange ideas made GITEX AI Europe an outstanding experience for our team.
Every conversation helped us better understand the evolving needs of engineering organizations and further validated the direction we're taking.
We're leaving Berlin energized by the feedback, inspired by the innovation we witnessed, and excited about the many new relationships we've started.

The momentum around AI-assisted software development is undeniable, but it's equally clear that success will depend on building systems that developers trust - systems that combine AI capabilities with human expertise, governance, and production-ready workflows.
We're excited to continue these conversations and work together with organizations looking to build the next generation of AI-powered software development.
If we met at GITEX AI Europe, thank you for stopping by. If we didn't have the chance to connect, we'd love to show you what we're building at Crodox.
See you at the next event!
